sentences.text: The only valid species within this extinct genus is Lesothosaurus diagnosticus.
This lightly built, bipedal animal measured between 1 and 2 meters in length.
Its skull featured large eye sockets that accounted for 36% of the skull's basal length.
Lesothosaurus possessed 15 to 16 tooth positions in its upper jaw, a higher count than the related Pisanosaurus.
Although no complete neck series has been preserved, the animal had only nine cervical vertebrae.
Evidence of rapid tooth replacement has been found in the back teeth of Lesothosaurus.
Preserved ossified tendons on the back vertebrae suggest the animal used them to counteract stress during bipedal movement.
The genus Lesothosaurus was named by paleontologist Peter Galton in 1978.
Fossils referable to Lesothosaurus may have been known as early as 1959.
The animal is known from at least four skeletons.
Lesothosaurus fossils are found in the red and white sandstones and mudstones of the Upper Elliot and Clarens Formations.
Likely a fast runner, the animal possessed long slender legs and a slender tail.
Lesothosaurus was likely an opportunistic omnivore that fed primarily on small animals when softer plants were unavailable.
The animal sliced its food with its beak but could not chew it.
Evidence from a 2016 bonebed suggests Lesothosaurus may have lived in groups.
Researchers suggest that high diversity among heterodontosaurids, including Lesothosaurus, indicates species partitioned food sources to avoid competition.
A 1991 redescription by Paul Sereno classified Lesothosaurus as a basal member of the order Ornithischia.
Later studies placed Lesothosaurus as the most basal member of Neornithischia, relating it to Agilisaurus, Hexinulsaurus, and Nanosaurus.
The Paleobi Database lists the parent group of Lesothosaurus as Thyreophora.
Lesothosaurus lived during the Early Jurassic period, specifically the Lower Jurassic Hettangian and Sinemurian ages.
These fossils date to approximately 199 to 190 million years ago, or roughly 200 to 190 million years ago.
Remains have been found in what is now South Africa and Lesotho, where the animal lived in warm and arid conditions.
It is debated whether Stormbergia is a valid species or a synonym of Lesothosaurus.
Some researchers debate whether Lesothosaurus belongs to Neornithischia or is instead an early thyreophoran related to armored dinosaurs.

A 2017 study by Baron, Norman, and Barrett argued that differences between Stormbergia and Lesothosaurus relate to growth, making Stormbergia a subjective junior synonym of Lesothosaurus and thus invalid.
